At the end of the test, you'll have two minutes to check your answers.

you as well. So tell me Mr Jakey, you are here because an investigation showed microscopic
hematuria? Yes, I was in the process of applying for a new job about I think six months ago and I
had to get a check-up for insurance purposes. That was when blood was found in a urine sample.
Okay and also you followed up with your GP, is that correct? Yes that is correct. Since that
initial analysis, my GP has run two additional tests that confirm what was previously found.
But you have not noticed any blood in your urine or any other urinary problems, right?
Yes, right. That is why I was quite shocked when I got the results from that insurance medical.
I mean, I consider myself a generally healthy person. I mean, if you were to ask me,
I'd say I was doing pretty good health-wise. No major medical issues or anything like that.
What about your relatives? Anyone had any problems with their kidneys? You know, renal disease?
Not that I'm aware of.
So, I have the results of some recent blood investigations that your GP recently had done.
Most of the items are within normal ranges, such as your haemoglobin and platelets.
Also, your glucose level looks good.
I feel a bit nervous coming here, actually. Was there anything out of the normal range?
A few things actually. We took your blood pressure at the beginning of the visit and it is quite high at 146 over 102.
As for your investigations, the level of urea was quite high and also creatine was out of the normal range.
Also, your level of gamma glutamyl transpeptidase is very high.
What is that last thing? I have no idea what it refers to.
Well, a high gamma glutamyl transpeptidase level is compatible with liver disease related to a high alcohol intake.
The recommended upper limit of alcohol consumption for men is 28 units per week.
I see. Well, I'm going to have to work on that. I often drink a few more units than that per week.
Yes, I would definitely recommend that. In fact, I think you need to completely abstain from alcohol for the time being.
So does my drinking have anything to do with what's wrong with me?
Or is something else going on?
Well, microscopic haematuria has many renal and neurological causes
such as prostatic disease or stones
but the renal impairment, which is indicated by the high urea and creatine levels
along with the hypertension, point to some form of chronic glomerulonephritis
which is an inflammation of the tiny filters of your kidneys
You can think about it like this. The tiny filters of your kidney work to remove excess fluid, electrolytes and waste from your bloodstream and pass them into your urine.
How concerned should I be? I mean, is this serious or long term?
Well, about 20% of patients with this condition will go on to develop end-stage renal failure within 20 years of first developing it.
So it is something that may affect you in the long run.
Also, this condition along with your declining liver function is very concerning.
We will need, I think, a liver ultrasound and probably also a biopsy to see the extent of the damage to your liver.
I see. So no more...
This is an edubenchmark.com sample test paper.
Extract 2. Questions 13 to 24. You hear a specialist talking to a patient referred by her GP.
For questions 13 to 24, complete the notes with a word or short phrase. You now have 30 seconds to look at the notes.
Hello Sheila.
I have the results of the electrocardiogram and chest x-ray that your GP sent you here
to get.
but first I just want to review your symptoms to get a complete picture.
Okay, sounds fine.
So you're a student, is that right?
Yes, in my last year of university.
And so when did the shortness of breath start?
About 10 days ago, I think.
At first it was after I rushed from one class to another or had to go upstairs.
I mean, I figured it was because I had not been exercising regularly lately.
After a couple of days, I couldn't even walk 50 yards without feeling out of breath.
And any recent illnesses, like the flu or bad cold?
Yes, about two to three days before I started feeling out of breath, I had a flu-like illness,
you know, with the normal generalised muscle aches and fever.
I rested for a day or two and then felt better, until I started my routine,
and that is when the breathlessness got worse, not better.
It's hard for me to wrap my head around it.
I mean, I'm still young, but I feel like sometimes I'm gasping for breath,
like a 90 year old running a marathon. I bet you are also feeling quite tired. Yes, how did you know?
I feel extremely tired at times and also I have noticed heart palpitations and some discomfort
in my chest along with breathlessness. I'm not sure if that is related to the breathlessness but...
Hmm, any changes in routine or lifestyle? I mean you said you thought the breathlessness might be
due to lack of exercise. I mean, it has been a tough semester at uni, so I have not been exercising
as much as I would like, but I still manage to go for a run two or three times a week.
Oh, okay. So you would say you are generally a fit person. And any experimentation with drugs?
No, no substance abuse. I mean, I know what you're thinking. Young person in uni must want
to experiment, but nope, that's not me. So what does all this mean? I mean, you have heard my
symptoms now and you have my tests. So your chest x-ray was normal which is good but I'm afraid
there are some abnormalities in your ECG. This along with the symptoms you described of fatigue,
shortness of breath, pericardial pain and palpitations points to myocarditis. The flu-like
illness you described is also compatible with this disease. I asked about substance abuse because one
cause of myocarditis is cocaine use. So... I see, I get it, you have to ask. Okay, so what does that
mean exactly, viral myocarditis? Is it something wrong with my lungs or my heart or...? Myocarditis
is an inflammation of the heart muscle and the viral part refer to the fact that a virus is the
cause. There are a number of viruses that can cause this problem including Coxsackie B and A,
echovirus and varicella.
Isn't varicella chickenpox?
Yes, it is.
So is this serious?
Well, first we'll need to perform an echocardiography to confirm the diagnosis
and we'll also do some investigations to test for the cause of the myocarditis.
Based on the fact that your chest x-ray was normal, the myocarditis is likely mild.
So that is the good news.
The maybe not so great news is that you will need to be on bed rest for a while.
Most cases of myocarditis are benign and cardiac function returns to normal,
but resting is an important part of treatment.
That will be a bit difficult,
but I will have to see what arrangements I can make at uni to lighten my load for the next.
That is the end of Part A. Now look at Part B.

Question 27. You hear part of an information session for the public about when to go to the A&E.
Now read the question.
Welcome everyone. I'm delighted that everyone could be here today to go over several topics
related to your healthcare. The first topic we're going to cover is when to go to the A&E.
So, an A&E department, which is also known as an emergency department or casualty,
deals with genuine life-threatening emergencies such as loss of consciousness, chest pain,
severe bleeding that cannot be stopped and stroke. Other serious emergencies including
severe allergic reactions and severe burns and scalds. Less severe injuries can be treated in
urgent care centres or minor care units. Most importantly the A&E is not an alternative to a
GP appointment. If you are experiencing changes in your health that you are concerned about,
it is essential that you make an appointment with your GP as he or she is best positioned to follow
your medical history and make the necessary referrals should you need specialised care.
Another reason that A&Es are often short-staffed, meaning that patients that are not going through
potentially life-threatening situations are taking away precious resources from those patients that
truly do need these resources. And finally…
Question 28. You hear part of a training for dentists about easing dental fear. Now read
the question.
Many people feel nervous or afraid of visiting the dentist, but as dentists there are a few
simple things we can do to help our patients overcome their fear. First is to be open to
having potential patients come and visit the surgery, meet the receptionist and you, the dentist,
in order to get a feel for the environment. If possible, make time to talk with anxious patients
about what their fears are. The next tip is to have your receptionist advise anxious or nervous
patients to pick an appointment time early in the morning so they have less time to dwell on their
feelings about the appointment. Speaking of this first appointment, it should be a check-up, not a
treatment as this will give the patient time to get comfortable with you and your staff.
During this check-up you may want to discuss with patients a sign to signal that they need a break
and that they want you to stop. It should be something simple like pointing your finger. This
will help the patient feel more in control of the situation. So some types of patients that
may be anxious or fearful of the dentist are.
Question 29. You hear part of a training for junior doctors.
Now read the question.
So you have made it through your medical training
and now you have been released into the world.
Now what?
How do you start to make your mark on the world?
It may feel as though you will be stuck in the role of Juna Doctor forever
and that there is nothing you can do about it.
But this series of training sessions is focused on skills
that you were not taught in your medical training,
but that are definitely necessary if you want to be successful in your medical practice.
So, the first session will deal with leading as a junior doctor within your organization.
Topics include how to successfully chair a meeting,
how best to negotiate with seniors and executives,
and how to use social media for the benefit of you and your colleagues.
So chairing a meeting, which is challenging and a skill that few receive any formal training for,
effective chairing is critical to ensure a successful meeting and require preparation and awareness of this role.
You need to know about the scope of the meeting, such as how essential the meeting actually is,
what the aims and desired objectives of the meeting are,
and what is the clearest and most concise way to achieve those aims.
Another consideration is who will attend the meeting.

Hello, well everyone, so as you are all probably aware, we are at capacity with no beds currently
available for incoming patients. So this means that patients experiencing a mental health
emergency are waiting in the emergency department for long periods of time. What the hospital has

While that is great news for patients, it will put a strain on nursing staff,
so we will need to continue to care for our current patients as well as those being admitted

I can make the necessary changes. Also a few nurses from other departments are being transferred to

about aspects of their work. For questions 31 to 42, choose the answer A, B or C which
fits best according to what you hear. Complete your answers as you listen.
Now look at extract 1.
Extract 1. Questions 31 to 36. You hear part of an interview about problems that junior
doctors face. You now have 90 seconds to read questions 31 to 36.
This is an EduBenchmark.com sample test paper.
Thank you.
Thank you.
So, hello Dr Stallings. It is nice to have you here today to talk about a topic that
has captured the attention of the nation, the plight of junior doctors in our national
healthcare system.
Yes, it is a very serious problem that has the potential to have a negative long-term
effect on healthcare in our country.
So tell me, what you see is the crux of the problem?
Hmm, it is definitely a complex problem. So coming to just one cause is not possible.
But what I would say is that morale among junior doctors in our country is at an all-time low,
which explains why resignations are rising, but also, sadly, why suicide among doctors is such a huge problem.
Well, resigning is one thing, but suicide is another matter altogether.
Why do you think this is such a problem among doctors?
It is mostly due to the pressures of our work. I mean, people who have trained to be doctors
are incredibly committed and passionate about what they do. So there is a tendency to try
work through the pressure until, of course, it becomes too much. Just a statistic that can help
to illustrate the severity of the situation. Female doctors are reported to be four times
more likely to die by suicide compared to females in the general population.
What do you think needs to be done to start to tackle this problem?
Well, the first thing is to acknowledge the problem.
One colleague recently wrote an interesting post in our prominent journal,
and her main point was that we need to stop the culture of shame
that is part of the culture of our national healthcare system
and come together to create safe spaces for staff to learn and reflect together.
It is somewhat ironic that it is our life's work to take care of others,
but we do not have structures in place to ensure the well-being of all staff.
So a few moments ago you mentioned resignations.
What do you think would lead a doctor who, as you stated,
starts off so full of enthusiasm for the profession to resign?
Well, in my experience, the number one reason is professional passivity.
You come full of energy and enthusiasm and you think you can change things for the better.
but then you confront the system.
You try to raise issues or concern and are met with walls.
Eventually being ignored leads to disengagement.
I see, I'd never thought of that.
So what do you think can be done to solve this particular problem?
Well, to remedy this, junior doctors must be encouraged
and enabled to be involved in professional development opportunities
such as leadership and research.
Many are not permitted to be involved in these activities
as the focus is on the provision of services.
While I understand there is a shortage of doctors, such as GPs,
forcing junior doctors to only focus on service provision is short-sighted.
Research by leading organisations has shown how important flexibility is
in maintaining doctors' well-being.
In addition, developing non-clinical skills is of utmost importance
for the future of training and healthcare as a whole.
Providing junior doctors with the opportunity to develop leadership and research skills could definitely improve trainee satisfaction and therefore improve retention and recruitment rates
So is it all gloom and doom for junior doctors or is there some hope?
No, no, of course there is some hope
In fact, things are on the cusp of improving
Junior doctors are coming together to advocate for quality improvement
and for learning about the managerial side of the job so that beneficial changes can be made.
For example, our focus group of junior doctors show that some places of work are putting into place new ways of developing ideas,
such as through regular meetings with the medical and managerial teams to highlight problems and work together to resolve them.
There are also some efforts that, while well-intentioned, need to be reviewed to make sure that they are effective as they can be.
For example, the mandatory e-learning modules need to be reviewed to look for ways that they can be made more flexible
and for ways that doctors can have more of a role in shaping their own training.
This would mean that junior doctors would engage more and stay in posts that are beneficial to their career,
and it would also allow for other, more practical activities,
such as discussing difficult cases, to be valued as learning activities.
What about mentoring schemes? Are they viewed favourably by junior doctors?
Oh yes, they certainly are. I was recently part of a mentoring scheme
and all the mentees and mentors found it very useful in their professional practice.
In particular, mentees said it helped them to feel more engaged
and that it was beneficial for their health.

response to a new virus, a virus that belongs to the large family of viruses known as coronaviruses.
Just to give us some background before getting into the details of the current outbreak,
coronaviruses are generally zoonotic, meaning they are transmitted between animals and people.
Rarely, animal coronaviruses can infect people and then spread between people,
such as with SARS, MERS and now the new virus, officially named SARS-CoV-2.
So, the first coronavirus outbreak that I'm going to discuss is SARS,
which was first reported in Asia in early 2003.
SARS stands for Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome.
The illness then went on to spread to more than two dozen countries
in North America, South America, Europe and Asia
before the SARS global outbreak was contained.
There have been no reported cases of SARS since 2004.
So patients with SARS reported high fevers and other symptoms,
including headache, an overall feeling of discomfort and body aches.
Some people also experienced mild respiratory symptoms at the outset,
and 10 to 20% of patients reported having diarrhoea.
After 2-7 days, some SARS patients went on to develop a dry cough and most developed pneumonia.
MERS stands for Middle East Respiratory Syndrome and it is a viral respiratory illness first reported in Saudi Arabia in 2012
and has since spread to several other countries including the United States.
Most people infected with MERS develop severe respiratory illness, including fever, cough and shortness of breath.
The animal source of MERS is likely to be camels, and studies have shown that direct contact with camels is a risk factor for human infection with MERS.
However, more research is needed to understand the interactions between humans and camels
in order to get a more complete picture of how transmission takes place.
Another important piece of information is that while there are ways to test a person for MERS
and there are treatments for the disease, there is currently no vaccine available to protect against MERS.
Like MERS and SARS, the SARS-CoV-2 is a beta coronavirus.
Early reports of the current virus linked the outbreak to a large seafood and live animal market in China,
suggesting animal-to-person spread.
Later, a growing number of patients reportedly had not had contact with animal markets,
marking the shift to person-to-person spread.
Person-to-person spread has been reported outside of China, including in the United States, Japan and other countries.
Most recently, other places have apparent community spread, meaning that some people have been infected, who are not sure how or where they became infected.
While both MERS and SARS are known to cause severe illness in people, there is still much unknown about the current virus.
Symptoms of the SARS-CoV-2 or what many media outlets are calling COVID-19 virus include fever, tiredness, dry cough and shortness of breath
Some patients also experience aches and pains, nasal congestion, runny nose, sore throat and diarrhoea
It is currently believed that symptoms may appear in as few as 2 days or as long as 14 days after exposure
This is based on what has been seen previously as the incubation period of MERS.
It is worth noting that while the risk of catching COVID-19, COVID-19, from a person with no symptoms is very low,
many infected people experience only mild symptoms, particularly in the early stages of the disease.
Currently, most people, about 80%, recover from the disease without needing special treatment,
but around 1 in 6 infected become seriously ill and develop difficulty breathing.
Older people and those with underlying medical problems, like high blood pressure, heart problems or diabetes,
are more likely to develop serious illness.
So far, about 2% of people with the disease have died.
It is worth noting that this fatality rate is much lower than that of SARS, which was
estimated at 14 to 15 percent, and then that of MERS, which has a fatality rate of approximately
35 percent.
However, the situation with the new virus is still evolving, and numbers may change
once more data is available.
Also, currently it is believed that the new virus is much more infectious than either
of the other coronaviruses that have been spread between humans,
which is part of the reason there are currently so many new cases identified each day.
As with MERS, there are currently no vaccine available.
There is also no specific antiviral medicine to prevent or treat COVID-19.
Possible vaccines and some specific drug treatments are under investigation
and are being tested through clinical trials.
The World Health Organisation is coordinating efforts to develop vaccines and…
